material: Gelatin silver print; mounted and with original window mat
provenance: Ruzzie Green, Art Director of Stehli Silks Corporation | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Note | During the 1920s, the Stehli Silks Corporation (headquartered in Switzerland and with an American office in Lancaster, Pennsylvania) commissioned various artists to create designs for reproduction on its silk fabrics. Edward Steichen and Ruzzie Green, an illustrator and designer for Stehli Silks, had a chance encounter in 1926 during a transatlantic crossing on the Isle de France. Green asked him to contribute to the company's well-received 'Americana' line, which resulted in Steichen's photographs of everyday objects arranged in repeating patterns, such as the present work featuring matchsticks and cigarettes. Steichen made other compositions from thread, tacks, eyeglasses, and sugar cubes - an example of which is in the collection of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York (1987.1100.217).

provenance: Acquired from the photographer by artist Tokio Ueyama (1889-1954) in 1927 or 1931 | By descent to Suye Ueyama, wife of the above, in 1954 | By descent to the brother of the above, in 1969 | By descent to Irene Tsukada Simonian, daughter of the above and niece of Tokio Ueyama, in 2006 | | Literature | cf. Conger 536-543 | | Exhibited | Museum of Modern Art, Wakayama, Japan, Transbordering: Migration and Art Across Wakayama and the U.S.A., 30 September - 30 November 2023 | | Note | The artist Tokio Ueyama (1889-1954) acquired this remarkable photograph directly from one of Edward Weston's solo exhibitions held in Los Angeles in either 1927 or 1931. It has been treasured by the Ueyama family for nearly a century. | | Ueyama, whose painting retrospective was recently on view at the Denver Art Museum, emigrated from Japan to the United States in 1908 and spent much of his life in Southern California until his death in 1954. He earned a degree in Fine Arts from the University of Southern California, studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, and subsequently explored Europe and Mexico on a Cresson Traveling Scholarship, during which time he developed a lifelong friendship with Diego Rivera. When Ueyama returned home to Little Tokyo in Los Angeles, he co-founded Shaku-do-Sha, a multi-disciplinary art association that hosted events and installations, including Weston's 1927 solo exhibition. | | Following up on the success of his first solo exhibition in L.A. in 1925, a second show was presented from 3 - 10 July 1927 at Shaku-do-Sha. On July 13 Weston noted in his Daybook: ". . . I am stimulated with many thoughts after the long considered Japanese exhibit which took place last week. Financially, it was the most successful showing I have had." (Part II, p. 29). | | Another exhibition was mounted on 14 November 1931 in the Japanese Quarter in Los Angeles. Weston's Daybook entry for this date reads: "Today under Ramiel's direction I open in the Japanese quarter, Los Angeles. He sent me an S.O.S. for nudes." (Part II, p. 233). | | While it remains unknown from which of these two exhibitions that Ueyama acquired this striking image of Bertha Wardell, a price sticker, annotated '2.00' in pencil, is adhered to its mount.

Gartner Jr. (1925-2011), the photographer's first studio manager | Acquired from the above by the present owner in 2011 | | Literature | Valentine Lawford, Horst: His Work and His World (New York, 1984), p. 249 | David Bailey and Martin Harrison, Shots of Style: Great Fashion Photographs (London: Victoria & Albert Museum, 1985), p. 41 | Irving Penn：Printemps des Arts de Monte Carlo (Sporting D'hiver de Monte-Carlo, 1986), pl. 1 | Irving Penn, Passage: A Work Record (New York, 1991), p. 21 | | Note | In this enigmatic group portrait taken at Horst P. Horst's bucolic Oyster Bay estate on Long Island, Irving Penn portrays eight of Vogue magazine's leading photographers—figures who shaped the visual identity of postwar fashion and editorial photography. The sitters include (from left to right) Serge Balkin, Sir Cecil Beaton, George Platt Lynes, Constantin Joffé, Horst, John Rawlings, Penn (holding the camera shutter release), and Erwin Blumenfeld. At the center of the composition the model Dorian Leigh poses with a large-format camera, a quiet nod to the collaborative dynamic between photographer and subject. | | Taken during the first decade of Penn's long and influential career at Vogue, this portrait stands as both a document of a particular artistic community and a meditation on creative voice. The group is presented as a cohort of distinctive identities unified by a shared visual mission. The gentle wilderness of the setting sharply contrasts with their typical work environment at a photo studio or set. | | Vogue Photographers anticipates Penn's later series of group portraits depicting employees from various professions, shot with similar visual rigor. In placing his fellow photographers in this context, Penn subtly elevates their status from commercial contributors to cultural artisans, documenting them with the same respect and clarity he would bring to workers across other fields. The image remains a rare and intimate window into the creative engine behind one of the most influential magazines of the twentieth century. | | A print of this image is in the collection of the National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (NPG.88.70.57). |

We decided to make up an ad on the spot. Our driver, who was also serving as Elliott's assistant, became the model. We went and got his nephew and put them on a bicycle and shot it that day. Elliott was able to grasp the idea quickly and turn it into a documentary photograph." (Elliott Erwitt, The Private Experience, p. 60) | | In his 1974 monograph on Erwitt, Sean Callahan elaborated on this picture: "The photograph ... retains a spontaneous charm in spite of the fact that the assistant had to pedal back and forth nearly 30 times until Erwitt was satisfied with the precise composition. The boughs of the trees overhead allow a funnel of light to direct the viewer's eye to the rider, whose legs are curiously cocked askew to suggest the way a provincial farmer, not a professional cyclist, would ride. The tiny passenger is perfect framed against his uncle's broad back. And all this came together at a precise focusing spot that Erwitt had marked with a stone on the pavement." (Elliott Erwitt, The Private Experience, p. 60)

He gave the albums to fellow members of the Corps, including Maj. Mackenzie, who went on to become its Chief of Engineers from 1904 to 1908. | | In 1990 Mackenzie's album was sold at Sotheby's New York, after which it was disassembled so that the individual prints could be sold privately. According to the inscription on the present work, this cyanotype is believed to have been included in Mackenzie's album. | | Bosse's cyanotypes rarely come to auction. This print is a vibrant example of the cyanotype process used to capture the expanding American landscape of the nineteenth century.

artwork_title: Selected Source Photographs for Andy Warhol's 1963-64 Silkscreened Paintings of 'Jackie' (Kennedy) and 'Car Crashes'
provenance: The Estate of Andy Warhol | Private Collection | Acquired from the above by the present owner, circa 1995 | | Literature | cf. Georg Frei and Neil Printz, eds., The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Paintings and Sculpture 1961-1963, Volume 1 (London: Phaidon, 2002), p. 464, figs. 274-275 | cf. Georg Frei and Neil Printz, eds., The Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Paintings and Sculpture 1964-1969, Volume 2A (London: Phaidon, 2004), p. 115, fig. 32 | | Note | Andy Warhol often used press, reference, and police photographs as templates for his 1950s drawings, many of which were made for his commercial and advertising assignments. It was not until 1962 that he took the career-defining leap of transferring photographs into silkscreens for use in his fine art paintings. | | The three press and reference photographs offered here provide insight into Warhol's selection process for the imagery seen in particular series - specifically his 'Serial Disasters' (1962-63), which includes his 'Car Crash' and 'Burning Car' paintings (see Andy Warhol Catalogue Raisonné, Vol. 1, nos. 342-361, 425-429, and 542-545). The two 'car crash' images in this lot are respectively date-stamped 'Sep-2'54' and 'May 1-'63', indicating that Warhol not only sourced older photographs dating back to the mid-1950s, but he was actively accumulating images of recent accidents. Although their subject matter strongly corresponds to the imagery ultimately chosen for the 'Car Crash' paintings, it is not believed that either of these photographs was transferred into silkscreen. | | The third photograph included in this lot relates to Warhol's 1964 'Jackie' paintings (AWCR, Vol. 2, nos. 937-1239), all based on press images taken on the day of President John F. Kennedy's assassination in Dallas on November 22, 1963. The present photograph is a slight variant of an image of Jackie taken before the assassination and featured in many works within this series (see 'Round Jackies', nos. 937-944; 'Multiplied Jackies', nos. 949-972, and 'Single Jackies', nos. 973-1054). | | This 'Jackie' print features red crop marks that correspond to the rectangular ratio of other images of her ultimately transferred to silkscreen. The reverse of this press print is annotated 'Onassis' in ink in an unidentified hand, indicating that it likely did not come into Warhol's possession until after Jackie married Aristotle Onassis in 1968. In fact, Warhol returned to the 'Jackie' theme around that time and perhaps acquired an additional selection of Jackie images after their marriage.
